passage: I'm Gargi, and I used to fight with my mother every single evening about homework. She'd say, "Sit now!" and I'd say, "Five more minutes!" and then we'd both be cross. Last month my mother, Neelam, tried something different. She said, "You can start at five or at six. Your choice. And you can pick which subject first." I picked six, because my cartoon ends at 5:55. I did Hindi first because it's the easiest. And the strange thing is, I actually sat down at six without her calling me even once. It felt like it was my plan. Now I set my own alarm on her old phone.

qa.q: Which subject did Gargi do first?
qa.a: Gargi did Hindi first because it's the easiest.

qa.q: Why did Gargi sit down at six without being called?
qa.a: Because Gargi had chosen the time, it felt like Gargi's own plan rather than an order, so there was nothing to fight about.

qa.q: What made Neelam's offer work, and what could come next?
qa.a: It gave real choices inside a limit, since homework still happens; next she might let Gargi plan the order for the whole week.

qa.q: How might evenings feel different for Neelam now?
qa.a: Neelam probably feels calmer, no longer calling and arguing, and can see her child taking charge of the evening.

grounding: A child describes how being offered a choice of study time and subject ended the nightly homework fight.

Note for Thursday's parents' circle, from Arohi (Kamal's mother).
For weeks, homework time with Kamal was a battle. I set the time, the order and the place, and he'd stall, sharpen pencils, lie on the floor. Last Monday I tried the suggestion from our last meeting. I said, "Maths or English first? And do you want to start at 4:30 or after your snack at 5?" He looked suspicious, then said, "English. At five." At five he sat down by himself and finished both subjects with only one reminder. He has chosen every day since, and yesterday he told his cousin, "I do English first, that's my system." What I did next: I stopped choosing for him, but I kept the rule that homework happens before play.

qa.q: What two choices did Arohi offer Kamal?
qa.a: Maths or English first, and starting at 4:30 or after his snack at 5.

qa.q: What does Kamal calling it 'my system' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: Kamal feels proud and in charge of homework now; because he picked the order and time, it feels like his idea rather than something done to him.

qa.q: What limit did Arohi keep, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She kept the rule that homework happens before play, so the choices are real but still sit inside a clear boundary.

qa.q: How might Kamal's cousin hear about Kamal's homework now?
qa.a: The cousin hears Kamal talk proudly about a 'system', which makes homework sound like something Kamal runs, not something forced on Kamal.

grounding: A mother's note records how offering two small real choices turned homework battles into cooperation.

Tuesday, 14 November
Dear Diary,
Big change today. Appa didn't shout "STUDY NOW" like always. Instead he asked, "Do you want to do science or social first? Before cricket or after dinner?" I was so surprised I just stared. Then I said science, after dinner, because cricket with Chaitanya is at 5 and it's the best part of the day.
And I actually did it! 7:30 to 8:30, science first, then social. Nobody had to call me. Appa just said, "Good plan," and went back to his newspaper.
Chaitanya says his dad decides everything, even which pen he uses. I told him to try asking for two choices. Maybe it works on all dads 🙂
Pradeep

qa.a: From 7:30 to 8:30, science first, then social.

qa.q: Why was Pradeep so surprised by Appa's question?
qa.a: Appa usually shouted 'STUDY NOW', so being asked to choose made Pradeep feel trusted, which was new.

qa.a: To ask his dad for two choices; small real choices make a child feel in charge, which makes cooperating easier.

qa.q: How might Appa feel after saying 'Good plan'?
qa.a: Appa may feel relieved that no shouting was needed, and pleased that Pradeep followed a plan Pradeep made.

Every evening in their house at the edge of a village near Satara, homework time began with a fight. Ritu would drag her slate, sulk and stare at the goats.
One evening Kalyani tried something new. She set two books on the mat, maths and Marathi. 'You choose. Which one first? And do you want to start now, or after we milk the goat?'
Ritu blinked. 'I can pick?'
'You can pick.'
Ritu thought hard. 'Marathi first. Now. Maths after the goat.'
She read her lesson aloud under the bulb without one complaint. After milking, she opened maths herself.
Kalyani said nothing, only smiled into the milk pail. The next evening Ritu was waiting on the mat before she was called.

qa.q: Which subject did Ritu choose to do first?
qa.a: Marathi, straight away, with maths after the goat.

qa.q: Why did Ritu ask 'I can pick?' in surprise?
qa.a: She wasn't used to having any say in homework; being given a real choice surprised her and made her feel trusted.

qa.q: Which choice of Kalyani's changed homework time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Offering two subjects and two times, all still within homework; Ritu felt in charge of her own evening, so the sulking stopped and she started without being told.

qa.q: How might homework time feel different for Kalyani now?
qa.a: Instead of a nightly fight, Kalyani finds a child already waiting on the mat, which likely feels calmer and more hopeful.

grounding: A mother lets her child choose which subject comes first and when to start, and the small real choice brings cooperation.

In their apartment in Curitiba, Jana used to groan the moment Priscila said the word 'homework'. Most evenings ended with a slammed door.
On Monday Priscila changed her script. She pinned a card to the fridge with two boxes: '4:30, before football' and '7:00, after dinner'. 'Homework happens every day,' she said. 'But you pick when. And you pick which subject goes first.'
Jana narrowed her eyes. 'Any time I want?'
'Either of these two. Your call.'
Jana ticked 4:30 and started with science, because the volcano chapter was fun. By Wednesday she was the one reminding Priscila: 'It's 4:30. I'm doing maths first today. Don't talk to me.'
Priscila hid a smile behind her coffee cup.

qa.q: What two times did Priscila write on the card?
qa.a: 4:30, before football, and 7:00, after dinner.

qa.q: Why was Jana suspicious at first?
qa.a: She was used to homework being ordered, so a real choice seemed too good to be true; she wanted to check how much say she actually had.

qa.q: Which part of Priscila's new plan made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Keeping homework daily but letting Jana choose the time and the first subject; she felt in charge, so she began reminding Priscila herself.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel on Wednesday when Jana says 'Don't talk to me'?
qa.a: Priscila seems amused and relieved, hiding a smile, since the evening fights have turned into Jana owning her homework. 😊

passage: At the community centre's homework room, Dhruv flopped onto the bench and crossed his arms. 'I'm not doing anything.' His father, Shankar, who helped out there on Tuesdays, sat down opposite him. He didn't argue. 'Okay. Maths first or Hindi first? Your call.' Dhruv peeked. 'Hindi.' 'And do you want to finish by six, or take a break at five-thirty and finish at six-fifteen?' Dhruv thought hard. 'Break.' He pulled out his Hindi notebook. Twenty minutes later he was still writing, tongue between his teeth. At the break he said, 'I picked Hindi first because it's easier to start.' Shankar nodded. 'Good thinking.' The maths was done by six-fifteen, without a single 'I'm not doing anything'.

qa.q: Which subject did Dhruv choose first?
qa.a: Dhruv chose Hindi first.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv start working once he was given a choice?
qa.a: Having a real choice made Dhruv feel in charge rather than ordered about, so his stubbornness eased and he felt willing.

qa.q: Why were Shankar's choices well designed?
qa.a: Both options got the homework done, so the limits stayed, but Dhruv had real say over order and timing, which increased cooperation.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Dhruv explains his choice?
qa.a: Shankar would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that his son had thought it through.

passage: I stay with my Mama's family in Guwahati during the holidays, so I see my cousin Tanvir's evenings up close. He's nine, and study time used to be a war. Mami would say, 'Books, now,' and he'd hide under the bed. This week something changed. Mami started asking, 'Science at five or at six? You pick.' Or, 'Reading or maths first?' The first day he stared at her as if it were a trick. Then he said, 'Six. And maths first.' At six he sat down on his own. I can't tell exactly what he's thinking, but he doesn't hide anymore, and yesterday he told me, very seriously, 'Bidisha, I decided the timetable.' Mami winked at me over his head. The work isn't less. It's the same pages. Only now he seems to feel they're his.

qa.q: What did Mami ask about science?
qa.a: She asked, 'Science at five or at six? You pick.'

qa.q: What does Tanvir's 'I decided the timetable' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and in charge, seeing study time as his own rather than something forced on him.

qa.q: What made Mami's approach work?
qa.a: She kept the limits, since study still happens, but gave Tanvir small real choices of time and order, so he cooperated instead of hiding.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see the change?
qa.a: Bidisha notices the war has stopped and he no longer hides, while admitting not knowing exactly what he is thinking.

passage:
Bidisha, you asked how I ever got through homework as a girl. Let me, your Nandini Dida, tell you.
I was ten, in Shillong, and I hated homework. Every evening my mother said, “Sit. Now.” And every evening I cried and sulked and did nothing.
Then one day she changed. She said, “You can do homework at five, before the radio programme, or at six-thirty, after it. You choose. And you can pick which subject first.”
I remember feeling suddenly grown-up. I chose six-thirty, and maths first, because I wanted it gone.
And I did it. Not happily every day, but without the war.
That small choice made me feel it was my homework, not hers. The work was the same. I was different.

qa.q: What were the two times young Nandini could choose?
qa.a: Five o'clock, before the radio programme, or six-thirty, after it.

qa.q: How did young Nandini feel when her mother offered the choice?
qa.a: She felt suddenly grown-up and trusted, as if the homework belonged to her.

qa.q: At what point in the story did the mother's choice change things?
qa.a: When she stopped saying “Sit. Now” and offered two times and which subject first, the daily fights ended.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother have felt when the crying stopped?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt relieved and pleased that a small choice worked better than orders.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a parent letting a child choose between two study times and which subject first, which increased cooperation.

passage:
The power had gone in the whole colony, the inverter was beeping, and Kavitha had exactly one hour of light before the battery died. Vikas, nine, had a Hindi test and a maths worksheet.
“Vikas, homework. Now.”
He flopped on the sofa. “No.”
Kavitha opened her mouth to shout, then stopped. The battery beeped again.
“Okay,” she said. “Hindi first or maths first? You choose.”
Vikas sat up a little. “Maths. It's shorter.”
“And do you want to sit at the table or on the floor by the window?”
“Floor.”
She handed him the torch as backup. He worked for forty minutes without a single complaint, pencil moving fast. When the inverter finally died, he was on the last sum.
“Done,” he said, and looked almost pleased with himself.

qa.q: How long did Kavitha have before the inverter battery died?
qa.a: She had exactly one hour of light.

qa.q: Why did Vikas sit up a little when his mother asked which subject first?
qa.a: He felt more in control and respected, like the homework was partly his decision.

qa.q: Which approach worked for Kavitha, and why?
qa.a: Offering two small real choices, subject order and where to sit, which made Vikas feel like an agent and led him to cooperate.

qa.q: What might have happened if Kavitha had kept shouting?
qa.a: Vikas might have dug in and sulked, wasting the hour of light in an argument.

grounding: The passage shows a parent under pressure giving a child small real choices about homework, which increases his cooperation.

Every Sunday in their Chennai flat was the same fight. Minakshi's mother, Gopika, wanted the weekly revision done. Minakshi, eleven, wanted to do anything else.
This Sunday, Gopika tried something new. She wrote two times on a slip: “11 a.m.” and “4 p.m.” Then three subjects: science, Tamil, social.
“Pick a time. And pick the order.”
Minakshi squinted at the slip, suspicious. “Really? Any order?”
“Any order. But all three, and at the time you pick.”
Minakshi chose 4 p.m., social first. At 3:58 she came to the table on her own, carrying her books.
Gopika said nothing, just put a glass of buttermilk next to her.
Minakshi worked for an hour and a half. Afterwards she said, “Can I choose again next week?”

qa.a: She wrote “11 a.m.” and “4 p.m.”

qa.q: Why did Minakshi come to the table on her own at 3:58?
qa.a: She felt trusted and in charge of her own decision, so doing the revision felt like her choice rather than an order.

qa.q: What small step helped end the Sunday fights?

The summer I was nine, Dida and I fought every afternoon over maths. One hot day, instead of calling me, Dida put two things on the table: my maths book and my English book. "You have to do both before the evening mango time. But you choose which one first, and whether you start at three or at four." I remember staring at her. Tutor's note, Christmas break, by Pallavi
Dhruv, age ten, fought every session last week. "I don't want to do science!" He'd kick the table leg until half the hour was gone.
This week I tried something different. I set out science and maths worksheets and said, "Both need doing today. You pick which first. And you pick: start now, or after a ten-minute snack?"
He narrowed his eyes. "Really?"
"Really."
He chose maths first, after the snack. At the ten-minute mark, he sat down on his own. No kicking. When he finished maths, he moved to science without being told.
What I did next: I'll keep offering two real choices at every session. He isn't choosing whether to work, only how. That seems to be enough.

qa.q: What did Dhruv choose to do first?
qa.a: He chose maths first, after the snack.

qa.q: What changed in how Dhruv felt when Pallavi offered choices?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and then more willing, feeling in control rather than ordered, so the kicking stopped.

qa.q: Why do Pallavi's two choices work inside a limit?
qa.a: Dhruv still has to do both worksheets, but choosing the order and start time makes him feel like an agent, not an object.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel after this session compared with last week?
qa.a: Pallavi was probably relieved and encouraged that the session went smoothly.

grounding: A tutor lets a boy choose which worksheet first and when to start, and small real choices within limits increase his cooperation.

Dear Diary,
Summer holidays, day 12. Hot hot hot.
Every day Papa says "Study now!" right in the middle of my game, and I shout and stomp and we both get cross. Today was different. Papa came and said, "Charu, holiday homework. You can do it at eleven, before lunch, or at five, after your nap. Your choice."
I picked five. Then he asked, "Maths first or Hindi first?" I said Hindi, because the story is nice.
At five I sat down by myself. Papa didn't even have to call me! I finished Hindi AND half the maths. Mummy laughed and said, "Pankaj, your trick worked."
It's funny. Same homework. But it felt like mine.
Charu
